target_audience: University students or advanced high school students (Calculus I)

sections.title: Prerequisite: Functions as Mappings
lecture_lines: Functions map values between two parallel number lines.
A point moving on the input line has a shadow.
This shadow moves along the output number line.
The function defines how these two movements relate.
We view functions as transformations, not just curves.
animations: Create two parallel horizontal number lines: Top (Input) in #FFFFFF, Bottom (Output) in #FFFFFF.
Create a green point 'x' (#00FF00) on the input line and its cyan image 'f(x)' (#00FFFF) on the output line.
Move 'x' smoothly to the right; animate 'f(x)' moving at a non-uniform speed to show the mapping relationship.

sections.title: Local Linearity: The 'Infinite Zoom'
lecture_lines: Zooming into a smooth function reveals a straight line.
Locally, any transformation behaves like a simple linear map.
This local view simplifies complex behavior into local stretches.
animations: Draw a curved function path in #555555 with a highlighted red point P (#FF0000) at (x, f(x)).
Perform a camera zoom onto point P until the curved path appears as a straight yellow line segment (#FFFF00).
Overlay a tangent line segment (#FFFF00) onto the curve at P to emphasize local linearity.
Define a small green interval 'dx' (#00FF00) on the input axis centered at P.
Project 'dx' through the mapping to show the cyan output interval 'df' (#00FFFF) on the output axis.

sections.title: The Derivative as a Scaling Factor
lecture_lines: The derivative measures the local scaling between lines.
Input changes by a tiny amount called dx.
Output changes by a corresponding amount called df.
The derivative f prime of x scales dx to df.
Thus, df equals f prime of x times dx.
animations: Show the Input and Output lines again. Highlight a fixed-length green segment 'dx' (#00FF00) on the Input line.
Project 'dx' to a cyan segment 'df' (#00FFFF) on the Output line. Display 'df = f\'(x) * dx' nearby.
Animate the transformation where f'(x) = 2: the 'df' segment stretches to double the length of 'dx' in #FF8800.
Animate the transformation where f'(x) = 0.5: the 'df' segment shrinks to half the length of 'dx' in #FF8800.
Flash the scaling factor 'f\'(x)' in #FF00FF to emphasize it as the multiplier between input and output.

sections.title: Visualizing Signs and Magnitudes
lecture_lines: Positive derivatives preserve the orientation of the line.
Negative derivatives flip the direction of the output.
Zero derivatives momentarily collapse the local segment.
animations: Animate 'dx' moving right; show 'df' moving right (#00FF00) and label 'f\'(x) > 0 (Preserves Direction)'.
Animate 'dx' moving right; show 'df' moving left (#FF0000) and label 'f\'(x) < 0 (Reverses Direction)'.
Animate 'dx' moving; show 'df' as a static point (#FFFF00) and label 'f\'(x) = 0 (Stationary/Compressed)'.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Dynamic Derivative
lecture_lines: The scaling factor changes as we move through domain.
This creates a dance of stretching and squishing.
High derivatives cause fast movement on the output.
Low derivatives cause slow crawling on the output.
This view provides a dynamic intuition for calculus.
animations: Show point 'x' (#00FF00) sliding across the entire input domain.
Animate the output point 'f(x)' (#00FFFF) accelerating and decelerating based on the varying scaling factor f'(x).
Show a graph of f'(x) in #FF8800 below the number lines, highlighting peaks (high stretch) and valleys (squish/flip).
